questions.prompt: `web.service` has `Requires=postgresql.service` and no `After=`. After every reboot it fails with `connection refused`, and starting it again by hand works. Why?
choices: Requires= is ignored during boot and only honoured for manual starts
postgresql.service is not enabled, so nothing starts it at boot
Requires= pulls postgresql in but orders nothing: both start at the same moment and web connects before postgres listens; it needs After=postgresql.service as well
The unit is missing Restart=always
questions.explanation: Requirement and ordering are two different axes. Requires= adds the dependency to the transaction and couples failures and stops; only After= makes this unit wait until the other has finished activating. By hand postgres is already up, so the race never shows.

questions.prompt: `db.service` is `Type=simple`. `web.service` has `After=db.service`. When exactly may web start?
choices: As soon as db's main process has been forked, whether or not db is ready to accept connections
When db has opened its listening port
When db has written its first line to the journal
When db's ExecStartPost has finished
questions.explanation: For Type=simple the manager considers the unit started right after the fork. Readiness needs Type=notify (READY=1 on $NOTIFY_SOCKET), or a oneshot that does the work before it exits, so After= on it means after the work.

questions.prompt: A unit with `Restart=on-failure` is killed with `kill -TERM <main pid>`. What does systemd do?
choices: Restarts it after RestartSec
Marks it failed (Result: signal) and leaves it down
Runs ExecStopPost and restarts it exactly once
Nothing: death by SIGTERM, SIGHUP, SIGINT or SIGPIPE is a clean exit, so the unit ends inactive (dead); only Restart=always would bring it back
questions.explanation: The clean-exit definition is exit status 0 (or a SuccessExitStatus=) or one of those four signals. on-failure restarts only on unclean exits, unclean signals, timeouts and watchdog hits; always restarts on every end except a stop requested through the manager.

questions.prompt: `systemctl status api` shows `failed (Result: start-limit-hit)` and the journal has five `Scheduled restart job` lines within four seconds. What happened and what is the first step?
choices: The disk is full; free space and start the unit

More than StartLimitBurst starts happened inside StartLimitIntervalSec, so the manager stopped restarting; read the exit code of the attempts in the journal, fix that cause, then systemctl reset-failed and start
RestartSec is too long; shorten it so the unit recovers faster
Raise StartLimitBurst so the unit keeps trying
questions.explanation: start-limit-hit is the rate limit, not the bug. The defaults are 5 starts in 10 seconds. The attempts' exit codes (status=1/FAILURE, 203/EXEC, a missing EnvironmentFile) name the real failure; the limit only decided when to stop looping.

questions.prompt: `systemctl stop api` takes 90 seconds on every deploy and the journal says `State 'stop-sigterm' timed out. Killing.` Which two keys describe the contract, and which side broke it?
choices: Restart= and RestartSec=: systemd restarted the service while stopping it
After= and Requires=: a dependency held the stop job back
KillSignal= (SIGTERM by default) and TimeoutStopSec= (90 s by default): the application ignored SIGTERM, the PID 1 lesson bug, so the manager escalated to SIGKILL and recorded Result: timeout
ExecStop= is mandatory and was missing from the unit
questions.explanation: Stop is SIGTERM to the whole control group, a bounded wait, then SIGKILL. A process that handles SIGTERM stops in milliseconds and the unit ends inactive (dead); one that ignores it costs the full timeout and ends failed (Result: timeout). Shortening TimeoutStopSec hides the symptom; the fix is the signal handler.

questions.prompt: You run `systemctl stop db.service`. `web.service` (`Requires=db.service`, `After=db.service`) is running, and so is `cache.service` (`Wants=db.service`). What happens?
choices: web.service is stopped first, then db.service; cache.service keeps running because Wants= does not propagate stops
Only db.service stops; stopping a unit never touches other units
All three stop, in the order they were started
web.service is restarted by its Restart=on-failure policy
questions.explanation: Requires= means an explicit stop of the dependency stops the dependent too, and ordering runs in reverse on the way down, so web goes before db. Wants= only pulls in on start. A stop requested through the manager also suspends the restart policy, the same rule your PID 1 supervisor had.
